Without a Y chromosome there is no male development. This describes Klinefelter.
This describes Turner syndrome (45,X).
trick: Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes minus 1.

q: Two genes 25 cM apart in a 3-point cross. Approximate recombination % between them?
why: One centimorgan equals 1% recombination, so 25 cM is about 25%.
traps: Too low. Map distance converts to percent one for one.
50% is the ceiling, seen for unlinked genes.
Recombination between two genes cannot exceed 50%.
trick: 1 map unit (centimorgan) = 1% recombination.

q: Coincidence (in 3-point cross) measures:
why: The coefficient of coincidence compares how many double crossovers actually appear with how many the two single-crossover rates predict. A value below 1 means one crossover interferes with a second nearby.
traps: That is recombination frequency.
Map distance is found from recombinant percentages.
Sister chromatid exchange creates no new combinations and is not what a three-point cross measures.
trick: Coincidence = observed double crossovers / expected. Interference = 1 - coincidence.

q: Hemophilia carrier mother × normal father, sons:
why: Each son gets one of his mother's two X chromosomes: half get the X with the hemophilia allele and are affected, half get the normal X.
traps: That would need a mother with the allele on both X chromosomes.
She carries the allele, so some sons are at risk.
A quarter is the chance for any child of either sex; among sons alone it is half.
trick: For X-linked crosses, write the sex chromosomes out. A son's X always comes from his mother; a father's X goes to every daughter.

q: Color blindness affected mother × normal father, outcome?
opts: All sons unaffected, all daughters affected
All sons affected, all daughters carriers
Half of sons and half of daughters affected
why: An affected mother has the allele on both X chromosomes. Every son gets one of them and a Y, so every son is affected. Every daughter gets one from her and a normal X from her father, so every daughter is a carrier.
traps: Reversed. Sons have only one X, from the mother, so they show the trait.
Her two X chromosomes are the same, so there is no 50-50 split.
Sons have no second X to mask the allele.
trick: For X-linked crosses, write the sex chromosomes out. A son's X always comes from his mother; a father's X goes to every daughter.

q: Codon AUG specifies:
why: AUG is the start codon, and it codes for methionine. Every new protein begins with it.
traps: The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA.
Valine codons start with GU.
Leucine has six codons, none of them AUG.
trick: AUG = start = methionine. Stops: UAA, UAG, UGA.

q: Codon UGA specifies:
why: UGA is one of the three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). No tRNA matches it, so translation ends.
traps: Tryptophan is UGG, one base away.
Methionine is AUG.
Cysteine is UGU or UGC, one base away.
trick: AUG = start = methionine. Stops: UAA, UAG, UGA.

q: A vector in cloning is:
opts: A plasmid that carries foreign DNA
The enzyme that cuts the DNA
The enzyme that copies the DNA
why: A vector is the carrier molecule, usually a plasmid or a virus, that takes a piece of foreign DNA into a host cell and gets copied there.
traps: That is the insert. The vector is what carries it.
That is a restriction enzyme.
That is a polymerase.
trick: Cloning cast: insert (cargo), vector (truck), restriction enzyme (scissors), ligase (glue).

q: Blue/white screening identifies:
opts: Colonies whose plasmid has an insert
why: The insert lands in the middle of the lacZ gene and breaks it. Colonies with an insert cannot make the enzyme and stay white; colonies with an intact plasmid turn the substrate blue.
traps: Color here reports on lacZ, not base composition.
The screen looks for a disrupted gene, not random mutations.
Antibiotic selection is a separate step that shows which cells took up any plasmid.
trick: Blue-white screening: white = insert present (lacZ broken).

q: cDNA libraries are made using:
why: cDNA is DNA copied from mRNA. Going from RNA back to DNA needs reverse transcriptase.
traps: DNA polymerase copies DNA from a DNA template, not from RNA.
Ligase joins DNA pieces; it copies nothing.
Restriction enzymes cut DNA.
trick: cDNA = mRNA copied backward by reverse transcriptase, so it has no introns.

q: Real-time qPCR measures:
opts: The base sequence of a gene
DNA quantity as it is amplified
The methylation state of a promoter
why: qPCR tracks fluorescence that rises with each cycle as copies are made. The sooner the signal appears, the more starting template there was, so it measures quantity.
traps: Reading the order of bases is sequencing.
Proteins are measured with a Western blot or ELISA.
Methylation needs other methods.
trick: PCR copies; qPCR counts.

q: STR (short tandem repeat) analysis is used for:
why: People differ in how many times short sequences repeat at certain sites. Comparing repeat counts at several sites gives a profile that identifies an individual or shows relatedness.
traps: Cloning uses vectors and restriction enzymes.
STR analysis measures fragment lengths; it does not read sequence.
It is an application of PCR, not a way to tune it.
trick: STRs: count the repeats, match the profile.

q: CRISPR-Cas9 PAM site is:
opts: A short motif beside the target
A stop codon that ends translation
A site where a repressor binds
why: The PAM is a short DNA sequence that must sit right next to the target site. Cas9 checks for it before cutting, which also keeps Cas9 from cutting the bacterium's own CRISPR array.
traps: Promoters are for transcription and are unrelated to Cas9.
Stop codons act during translation.
Repressor sites belong to operons.
trick: CRISPR = guide RNA finds the address, Cas9 cuts, and only next to a PAM.

q: Stem cells differ from differentiated cells in:
why: Stem cells can divide to make more stem cells (self-renewal) and can also give rise to specialized cell types (potency). Differentiated cells have lost both abilities.
traps: Most differentiated cells have a nucleus too.
Size does not define a stem cell.
Stem cells have mitochondria.
trick: Stem cell = self-renew + differentiate.

q: Wild-type allele is usually:
why: Wild type means the version of a gene most often found in natural populations. It is the reference against which mutant alleles are named.
traps: Wild type is defined by frequency, and it is more often dominant than recessive.
A new mutant is by definition not the wild type.
Wild type is the normal working version.
trick: Wild type = the common, standard allele.

q: Penetrance of an allele refers to:
opts: How many offspring inherit the allele
Share of carriers showing the trait
why: Penetrance is the percent of individuals with a genotype who actually show the expected phenotype. If 80 of 100 carriers show it, penetrance is 80%.
traps: Inheritance odds come from the cross, not from penetrance.
Severity is expressivity.
Range of severity is also expressivity.
trick: Penetrance: whether it shows (yes or no). Expressivity: how strongly it shows.

q: Expressivity refers to:
opts: The number who show the trait
The range of severity among those with it
The equal expression of both alleles at once
why: Expressivity describes how much the phenotype varies among people who have the same genotype and do show the trait: mild in one person, severe in another.
traps: That is penetrance.
Allele frequency is a population measure.
That is codominance.
trick: Penetrance: whether it shows (yes or no). Expressivity: how strongly it shows.

q: Spontaneous abortions are most often associated with:
why: About half of early miscarriages involve a chromosome number error, and trisomies are the most common kind. Most trisomies are not compatible with development.
traps: Translocations cause some losses but are far less common.
Single base changes rarely end a pregnancy.
Inversions usually keep all the genes and are often harmless.
trick: Wrong chromosome number is usually lethal; only a few trisomies (21, 18, 13) reach birth.

q: Why is X-inactivation important in XXY males (Klinefelter)?
opts: It does not occur in males
why: Any cell with more than one X silences the extras. An XXY male has two X chromosomes, so one is inactivated and shows up as a single Barr body.
traps: It depends on the number of X chromosomes, not on sex.
Only one X stays active per cell.
The Y is never the target of X-inactivation.
trick: Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes minus 1.

q: Synaptonemal complex forms during:
why: The synaptonemal complex is the protein zipper that holds homologous chromosomes together during pairing in prophase I, which is when crossing over takes place.
traps: Homologs do not pair in mitosis.
By meiosis II the homologs are in different cells.
By meiosis II the homologs are in different cells.
trick: Anything about pairing of homologs (synapsis, tetrads, chiasmata) is prophase I.

q: Why are spermatids haploid?
why: A primary spermatocyte (diploid) goes through meiosis I to make two secondary spermatocytes, and meiosis II splits those into four spermatids, each with one set of single chromosomes.
traps: Mitosis keeps cells diploid.
The halving is a regular outcome of meiosis, not chance.
Spermatids carry one set of chromosomes.
trick: Spermatogonium, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, sperm: meiosis I and II sit in the middle.

q: A test cross of AaBbCc × aabbcc gives how many genotype classes?
why: The triple heterozygote makes 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 kinds of gametes. The aabbcc parent makes only one kind, so there are 8 offspring classes.
traps: That is two genes: 2 x 2.
That is four genes: 2 to the fourth.
27 is 3 cubed, the genotype count when both parents are triple heterozygotes.
trick: Gamete types from a heterozygote: 2 to the power of the number of heterozygous genes.

q: Probability of three offspring being all male:
why: Each birth is independent with a 1/2 chance of a boy. All three: 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8.
traps: That is two boys in a row.
That is one birth.
That is the chance of exactly one boy (or exactly two) in three births.
trick: Independent events in a row: multiply.

q: Probability of at least one of 3 children being female:
why: The only way to miss is three boys: (1/2) cubed = 1/8. So at least one girl is 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.
traps: That is the chance of no girls. Subtract it from 1.
That is one birth. Three tries raise the odds.
That is the chance with two children, not three.
trick: At least one = 1 minus none.

q: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA by:
why: All DNA carries the same negative charge per unit length, so every fragment is pulled toward the positive end. The gel is a mesh: short fragments slip through faster and travel farther.
traps: Charge is why DNA moves, but it is the same for every fragment, so it cannot sort them.
Standard gels do not sort by base composition.
Two fragments of equal length with different sequences run together.
trick: Gel: small runs far, large stays near the well.

q: Western blot detects:
why: A Western blot separates proteins by size and then uses an antibody to find one specific protein.
traps: DNA is detected by a Southern blot.
RNA is detected by a Northern blot.
Lipids are not what blots detect.
trick: Blots by molecule: Southern DNA, Northern RNA, Western protein.

q: Aneuploidy vs polyploidy:
opts: They are two words for one thing
Aneuploidy: single chromosomes; polyploidy: whole sets
Aneuploidy: whole sets; polyploidy: single chromosomes
Aneuploidy: a duplication; polyploidy: a point mutation
why: Aneuploidy is one chromosome too many or too few (2n + 1 or 2n - 1). Polyploidy is one or more complete extra sets (3n, 4n).
traps: They differ in scale: one chromosome versus a whole set.
Reversed: aneuploidy is the single-chromosome change.
Both are changes in chromosome number, not changes within a chromosome.
trick: Aneuploid: off by one. Polyploid: off by a whole set.

q: In a pedigree, two parents who both show a genetic condition have a child who does not show it. Which mode of inheritance best explains this family?
opts: Y-linked, passed from father to every son
Autosomal dominant from a new mutation
Autosomal recessive, with both parents homozygous
why: Two affected parents with an unaffected child means the unaffected state was hidden in both parents, so the condition is dominant and both parents are Aa. The child is aa.
traps: Y-linked would pass from the father to every son and could not come from the mother.
A new mutation is not needed; two heterozygotes explain it directly.
If both parents were homozygous recessive, every child would be affected.
trick: Two affected parents, unaffected child: dominant. Two unaffected parents, affected child: recessive.

q: Mosaicism describes:
opts: One body with two cell lines
why: A mosaic is one individual whose cells are not all genetically the same, because a mutation or chromosome error happened in one cell after fertilization and was passed to its descendants.
traps: Identical twins are two individuals with matching genomes.
That is polyploidy.
That is pleiotropy.
trick: Mosaic = change after fertilization, so only some cells carry it.

q: Mendel chose pea plants because:
why: Peas come in true-breeding lines with clear either-or traits (tall or short, round or wrinkled), and their pollination is easy to control, so offspring could be sorted and counted cleanly.
traps: The pea genome is large, and Mendel knew nothing of genomes.
Being diploid is true of most plants and animals, so it was not a reason to pick peas.
Peas do need pollination; the advantage is that it can be controlled.
trick: Mendel's edge: discrete traits, pure lines, controlled crosses, large counts.

q: Insertion of 3 bases mid-gene typically causes:
why: Three bases make exactly one codon. Inserting three bases adds one amino acid and leaves the reading frame downstream intact.
traps: A frameshift needs a number of bases that is not a multiple of three.
A stop codon would only arise if the inserted bases happened to spell one.
The protein is one amino acid longer, so it does change.
trick: Point mutations: silent (same amino acid), missense (different one), nonsense (stop). Insertions or deletions not in threes shift the frame.

q: Which chamber receives oxygenated blood from the lungs?
why: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, which then passes it to the left ventricle.
traps: The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the body.
The right ventricle pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
The left ventricle gets this blood second, from the left atrium, and pumps it to the body.
trick: Trace one loop: body, right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle, body. Right side handles oxygen-poor blood.

q: Which vessel carries DEoxygenated blood?
why: The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, before it has picked up oxygen. It is the one artery that carries oxygen-poor blood.
traps: The aorta carries freshly oxygenated blood to the body.
The pulmonary vein brings oxygen-rich blood back from the lungs.
Coronary arteries branch off the aorta and carry oxygen-rich blood to heart muscle.
trick: Arteries leave the heart, veins return to it. The pulmonary pair is the one place where the oxygen labels flip.

q: S1 ("lub") sound is caused by closure of:
why: When the ventricles start to contract, pressure snaps the tricuspid and mitral valves shut so blood cannot flow back into the atria. That closure is the first heart sound.
traps: The aortic valve closes at the end of systole and contributes to the second sound.
The pulmonary valve also closes at the end of systole.
Semilunar valves closing make S2, the 'dub'.
trick: S1 lub = AV valves close (systole starts). S2 dub = semilunar valves close (systole ends).

q: The heart's pacemaker is the:
why: The sinoatrial node in the right atrium fires on its own faster than any other part of the heart, so it sets the rhythm for the rest.
traps: The AV node delays the signal and passes it on; it only sets the pace if the SA node fails.
The bundle of His carries the signal down the septum.
Purkinje fibers spread the signal through the ventricles.
trick: Conduction order: SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers.

q: During inhalation, the diaphragm:
why: The diaphragm contracts and flattens downward, which enlarges the chest cavity. Bigger volume means lower pressure, and air flows in.
traps: That is exhalation: the relaxed diaphragm domes upward.
Quiet breathing depends on the diaphragm moving.
The diaphragm moves up and down, not sideways.
trick: Inhale: diaphragm contracts and drops, pressure falls, air enters (negative pressure breathing).

q: A right shift of the oxy-Hb curve indicates:
why: A right shift means hemoglobin holds oxygen less tightly at any given oxygen level, so it releases more to the tissues. Heat, acid, CO2 and 2,3-BPG all cause it, which fits a working muscle.
traps: Higher affinity is a left shift.
The curve moved, so affinity changed.
The shift describes hemoglobin's grip, not how much oxygen is in the blood.
trick: Right shift = release. Causes: more CO2, more acid, more heat, more 2,3-BPG.

q: Which cells produce surfactant?
why: Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension so the alveoli do not collapse.
traps: Type I cells are the thin cells where gas exchange happens.
Goblet cells make mucus in the airways.
Macrophages clean up debris in the alveoli.
trick: Type I = exchange surface. Type II = surfactant.

q: During depolarization of a neuron, which ion enters?
why: At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na+ floods in down its gradient, driving the inside of the cell positive.
traps: K+ leaves the cell during repolarization; it does not enter.
Ca2+ entry matters at the axon terminal for transmitter release, not for the upstroke.
Cl- entry would make the cell more negative, the opposite of depolarization.
trick: Action potential: Na+ rushes in to rise, K+ flows out to fall. Na+ channels then sit inactivated for a moment.

q: Why is the action potential all-or-nothing?
opts: The Na/K pump fires only once
Na+ entry opens more Na+ channels
K+ exit happens in fixed steps
The neuron dies if it fails
why: Once threshold is reached, incoming Na+ depolarizes the membrane further, which opens still more voltage-gated Na+ channels. That positive feedback runs to completion every time, so the spike is always full size.
traps: The pump works continuously to maintain gradients; it does not create the spike.
K+ exit ends the spike; it is not what makes it all-or-nothing.
A neuron that stays below threshold simply does not fire.
trick: Action potential: Na+ rushes in to rise, K+ flows out to fall. Na+ channels then sit inactivated for a moment.

q: During absolute refractory period:
why: Right after opening, voltage-gated Na+ channels close an inactivation gate and cannot reopen until the membrane resets. No stimulus, however strong, can fire the cell during that time.
traps: Only a tiny number of ions move per spike; the gradient barely changes.
The pump does not tire out between spikes.
K+ channels are open in this period; that is what repolarizes the cell.
trick: Action potential: Na+ rushes in to rise, K+ flows out to fall. Na+ channels then sit inactivated for a moment.

q: Which nephron segment is impermeable to water?
why: The ascending limb pumps salt out but has no water channels, so water cannot follow. That is how the filtrate becomes dilute while the medulla becomes salty.
traps: The proximal tubule reabsorbs most of the water.
The descending limb is the water-permeable side of the loop.
The collecting duct lets water through when ADH is present.
trick: Loop of Henle: descending lets water out, ascending lets salt out.

q: ADH (vasopressin) acts on:
why: ADH makes collecting duct cells insert aquaporin water channels, so water leaves the urine and returns to the blood.
traps: The proximal tubule reabsorbs water without needing ADH.
The loop sets up the gradient; ADH acts further along.
The glomerulus only filters.
trick: ADH = add water channels to the collecting duct, so urine gets concentrated.

q: Aldosterone primarily increases:
why: Aldosterone tells the distal tubule and collecting duct to reclaim sodium and secrete potassium. Water follows the sodium, which raises blood volume and pressure.
traps: Direct water reabsorption is the job of ADH. With aldosterone, water only follows sodium.
Glucose is reclaimed in the proximal tubule without hormone control.
Aldosterone is about sodium and potassium, not bicarbonate.
trick: Aldosterone saves sodium and spends potassium. ADH saves water.

q: Insulin is produced by:
why: Beta cells in the pancreatic islets release insulin when blood glucose rises.
traps: Alpha cells make glucagon, which raises blood glucose.
Delta cells make somatostatin.
The adrenal cortex makes steroid hormones such as cortisol.
trick: Islets: alpha glucagon, beta insulin, delta somatostatin.

q: Which gland produces ADH and oxytocin?
why: Neurons in the hypothalamus make ADH and oxytocin and send them down their axons to the posterior pituitary, which stores and releases them.
traps: The anterior pituitary makes its own set of hormones (GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin).
The thyroid makes T3, T4 and calcitonin.
The adrenal cortex makes steroids.
trick: Posterior pituitary only stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, which the hypothalamus makes. Everything else pituitary is anterior.

q: PTH and calcitonin have what relationship?
why: PTH raises blood calcium and calcitonin lowers it. Two hormones pushing one variable in opposite directions are antagonists.
traps: Synergistic hormones push the same way.
They regulate the same variable, so they are not independent.
Sharing targets does not describe how they relate; their effects are opposite.
trick: Calcium: PTH pulls it up, calcitonin tones it down.

q: During muscle contraction, which sarcomere region remains constant in length?
why: The A band is the full length of the thick filament, and filaments do not change length when they slide. So the A band stays the same.
traps: The I band (thin filament only) narrows as thin filaments slide inward.
The H zone (thick filament only) narrows and can vanish.
The whole sarcomere shortens; that is the contraction.
trick: When a sarcomere shortens, the filaments slide and do not shrink: A band constant, I band and H zone narrow.

q: Which ion triggers muscle contraction by binding troponin?
why: Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin off the binding sites on actin so myosin can attach.
traps: Na+ carries the action potential along the membrane but does not bind troponin.
K+ repolarizes the membrane.
Cl- has no role at troponin.
trick: Calcium binds troponin, tropomyosin moves, myosin grabs actin.

q: HCl in the stomach is produced by:
why: Parietal cells in the stomach lining pump out hydrochloric acid (and make intrinsic factor).
traps: Chief cells release pepsinogen.
Goblet cells make protective mucus.
G cells release gastrin, the hormone that tells parietal cells to work.
trick: Stomach cells: parietal = acid, chief = pepsinogen, G = gastrin.

q: Pancreatic enzymes are activated by:
why: The pancreas ships its protein-digesting enzymes in inactive form. Enterokinase on the intestinal lining converts trypsinogen to trypsin, and trypsin then activates the rest.
traps: Pancreatic juice never enters the stomach; acid activates pepsinogen instead.
Gastrin drives acid secretion.
The liver makes bile, which holds no activating enzymes.
trick: Zymogens are switched on where they are needed: pepsinogen by acid, trypsinogen by enterokinase.

q: Bile is produced by the:
why: Liver cells make bile. The gallbladder only stores and concentrates it.
traps: The pancreas makes enzymes and bicarbonate.
The gallbladder stores bile but does not make it.
The small intestine receives bile.
trick: Liver makes bile, gallbladder stores it, CCK releases it.

q: Which cells present antigen on MHC class II?
why: MHC II is found only on professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells). They display pieces of what they have engulfed to helper T cells.
traps: All nucleated cells carry MHC I, not MHC II.
Cytotoxic T cells read MHC I; they do not present on MHC II.
Red blood cells have no nucleus and no MHC.
trick: MHC I is on all nucleated cells and talks to CD8 cells (1 x 8 = 8). MHC II is on antigen-presenting cells and talks to CD4 cells (2 x 4 = 8).

q: Antibodies are produced by:
why: An activated B cell matures into a plasma cell, a factory that secretes large amounts of antibody.
traps: Helper T cells release signals that activate B cells but make no antibody.
Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly.
Macrophages engulf pathogens.
trick: B cell becomes plasma cell (antibody now) or memory cell (antibody faster next time).

q: Which antibody class crosses the placenta?
why: IgG is the only class carried across the placenta, giving the newborn the mother's protection for its first months.
traps: IgA is in secretions such as milk and saliva.
IgM is a large pentamer and too big to cross.
IgE handles allergies and parasites.
trick: Antibody classes: G crosses the placenta, A guards mucosa, M comes first, E allergies, D sits on B cells.

q: The LH surge triggers:
why: A sharp rise in LH at mid-cycle makes the mature follicle rupture and release its egg.
traps: Menstruation follows the fall of progesterone at the end of the cycle.
Implantation comes about a week after fertilization.
Fertilization needs sperm; LH only releases the egg.
trick: Menstrual cycle: FSH grows the follicle, estrogen rises, the LH surge releases the egg, the corpus luteum makes progesterone.

q: hCG (basis of pregnancy tests) maintains:
why: hCG from the early embryo acts like LH and keeps the corpus luteum alive. The corpus luteum keeps making progesterone, which maintains the uterine lining.
traps: hCG protects the lining only indirectly, through progesterone from the corpus luteum.
The pituitary is not its target.
The placenta takes over progesterone production later; hCG's target is the corpus luteum.
trick: Menstrual cycle: FSH grows the follicle, estrogen rises, the LH surge releases the egg, the corpus luteum makes progesterone.

q: Spermatogenesis differs from oogenesis in that:
opts: It yields the same number of gametes
It also pauses in prophase I
It also yields one viable gamete
why: Sperm production runs continuously from puberty on. Oocytes all begin meiosis before birth, and no new ones are started afterward.
traps: Each meiosis gives four sperm but only one egg.
Only oocytes pause in prophase I.
Spermatogenesis gives four working gametes per meiosis.
trick: Sperm: continuous from puberty, four per meiosis. Eggs: started before birth, paused twice, one per meiosis.

q: Osteoclasts originate from:
why: Osteoclasts are large bone-resorbing cells formed by fusion of cells from the monocyte and macrophage line, which comes from blood-forming stem cells.
traps: Osteoblasts build bone and become osteocytes, not osteoclasts.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells.
Fibroblasts make connective tissue fibers.
trick: Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts break it down, osteocytes maintain it.

q: Vitamin D synthesis begins in the:
why: UV light on the skin converts a cholesterol-derived molecule into vitamin D3. The liver and then the kidney modify it into the active form.
traps: The liver does the second step.
The kidney does the final activating step.
The stomach is not involved.
trick: Vitamin D: skin starts, liver continues, kidney activates.

q: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by:
why: Brain capillary cells are sealed by tight junctions, and astrocytes wrap those capillaries with their end-feet and maintain the seal. Of the glial cells listed, astrocytes are the ones tied to the barrier.
traps: Microglia are the brain's immune cells.
Schwann cells make myelin in the peripheral nervous system.
Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the central nervous system.
trick: Glia: astrocytes support and seal, microglia defend, oligodendrocytes (CNS) and Schwann cells (PNS) myelinate.

q: Cardiac output = stroke volume × ?
why: Cardiac output is the volume pumped per minute: volume per beat (stroke volume) times beats per minute (heart rate).
traps: Blood pressure equals cardiac output times resistance; it is a result, not a factor.
Vessel diameter sets resistance.
Hematocrit is the fraction of blood that is red cells.
trick: CO = SV x HR. Then BP = CO x resistance.

q: P wave on EKG represents:
why: The P wave is the electrical signal spreading across the atria just before they contract.
traps: That is the QRS complex.
That is the T wave.
The AV delay is the flat stretch between the P wave and the QRS.
trick: EKG: P = atria depolarize, QRS = ventricles depolarize, T = ventricles repolarize.

q: During systole, which valves close?
why: As the ventricles contract, pressure inside them rises above atrial pressure and shuts the tricuspid and mitral valves, so blood can only leave through the arteries.
traps: Semilunar valves open during systole to let blood out.
Two valves must stay open or blood could not leave.
Without valve closure, blood would flow backward into the atria.
trick: Systole: AV valves shut, semilunar valves open. Diastole: the reverse.

q: Frank-Starling law states:
why: The more the ventricle is stretched by returning blood, the more forcefully it contracts, so the heart pumps out what it receives.
traps: The law is about stroke volume, not rate.
That is not a physiological law; pressure and flow are linked through resistance.
That is the blood pressure equation, a different relationship.
trick: Frank-Starling: stretch in, force out.

q: Coronary arteries supply:
why: The coronary arteries branch off the base of the aorta and feed the heart wall itself, which cannot use the blood passing through its chambers.
traps: The carotid and vertebral arteries supply the brain.
The pulmonary and bronchial arteries serve the lungs.
The hepatic artery and portal vein supply the liver.
trick: Corona means crown: the coronaries circle the heart.

q: Erythrocytes (RBCs) in mammals are:
why: Mature mammalian red blood cells eject their nucleus and organelles, leaving more room for hemoglobin.
traps: They have no nucleus at all. Skeletal muscle fibers are the multinucleate cells.
They also lack mitochondria and rely on glycolysis.
With no nucleus they cannot divide; new ones come from bone marrow.
trick: Mature RBC: no nucleus, no mitochondria, all hemoglobin.

q: Most abundant white blood cell type:
why: Neutrophils make up more than half of circulating white cells and are the first phagocytes to arrive at an infection.
traps: Lymphocytes are second most common.
Monocytes are a small share; they become macrophages.
Basophils are the rarest.
trick: White cell order, most to least: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils.

q: Universal blood donor type:
why: O negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigens, so no recipient's antibodies have anything to attack.
traps: A positive cells carry A and Rh antigens.
AB positive is the universal recipient, the opposite role.
B negative cells carry the B antigen.
trick: Universal donor O negative (no antigens). Universal recipient AB positive (no antibodies).

q: Clotting cascade ends with:
why: The cascade's last step is thrombin cutting fibrinogen into fibrin, whose strands form the mesh that stabilizes the clot.
traps: Factor X activation is a middle step that leads to thrombin.
The platelet plug forms first, before the cascade finishes.
Vitamin K is needed to make several factors; it is not a step in the cascade.
trick: Clot order: platelet plug, then prothrombin to thrombin, then fibrinogen to fibrin.

q: Fetal foramen ovale connects:
why: The fetus does not breathe, so blood entering the right atrium passes through this opening straight into the left atrium and skips the lungs.
traps: Direction reversed. Fetal pressure is higher on the right side.
No normal fetal shunt joins those two.
The ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary artery to the aorta, flowing the other way.
trick: Two fetal shortcuts skip the lungs: foramen ovale (right atrium to left atrium) and ductus arteriosus (pulmonary artery to aorta).

q: Tidal volume is:
why: Tidal volume is the air moved in or out in one quiet, normal breath, about half a liter.
traps: Total lung capacity is everything the lungs can hold.
That is residual volume.
Vital capacity is the most air you can move in one maximal breath.
trick: Tidal = quiet breath. Vital = biggest breath. Residual = cannot be exhaled.

q: Residual volume is:
why: Even after the hardest exhale some air stays in the lungs and keeps the alveoli open. That leftover is the residual volume.
traps: That is tidal volume.
That is vital capacity.
That is anatomical dead space.
trick: Tidal = quiet breath. Vital = biggest breath. Residual = cannot be exhaled.

q: Most CO₂ in blood is transported as:
why: Inside red cells, carbonic anhydrase combines CO2 with water; the product splits into H+ and bicarbonate, and about 70% of CO2 travels in plasma as bicarbonate.
traps: Only a small share stays dissolved.
About a fifth rides on hemoglobin.
Carbonic acid forms only for an instant before it splits.
trick: CO2 + H2O gives H2CO3 gives H+ + HCO3-. Most CO2 rides as bicarbonate.

q: Hyperventilation causes:
why: Breathing fast blows off CO2. Less CO2 means less carbonic acid and fewer H+ ions, so blood pH rises: alkalosis from a respiratory cause.
traps: Acidosis comes from holding CO2 in, as in slow breathing.
The cause here is breathing, not metabolism, and pH rises.
CO2 and pH are tightly linked.
trick: CO2 is an acid in the blood: blow it off and pH rises; retain it and pH falls.

q: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) compared to adult HbA:
why: Fetal hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly than adult hemoglobin, so oxygen moves from the mother's blood to the fetus across the placenta.
traps: If it were lower, oxygen would flow the wrong way.
With equal affinity there would be no net transfer.
It carries oxygen for the fetus.
trick: Fetal hemoglobin sits to the left of the adult curve: tighter grip.

q: Medulla chemoreceptors primarily sense:
why: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H+ in the surrounding fluid, which tracks blood CO2. Rising CO2 is the main drive to breathe.
traps: Low oxygen is sensed mainly by peripheral receptors in the carotid and aortic bodies.
Glucose is monitored by the pancreas.
Temperature is monitored by the hypothalamus.
trick: The urge to breathe comes from CO2, not from lack of oxygen.

q: Resting membrane potential is approximately:
why: A resting neuron sits near -70 mV: the inside is negative because K+ leaks out and the Na+/K+ pump moves more positive charge out than in.
traps: +30 mV is roughly the peak of an action potential.
0 mV is passed through on the way up, not held at rest.
+70 mV is not reached.
trick: Rest -70, threshold about -55, peak about +30.

q: After neurotransmitter released, the action potential propagates by:
why: Depolarization at one spot brings the next patch of membrane to threshold, opening its voltage-gated channels, and so on down the axon like a line of dominoes.
traps: Simple diffusion would fade within a short distance.
Cytoplasm does not flow to carry the signal.
The membrane stays put; only ions and voltage change.
trick: Action potential: Na+ rushes in to rise, K+ flows out to fall. Na+ channels then sit inactivated for a moment.

q: Acetylcholine in the parasympathetic system acts at:
why: At parasympathetic target organs, acetylcholine binds muscarinic receptors.
traps: Adrenergic receptors bind norepinephrine and epinephrine (sympathetic).
GABA receptors bind GABA in the brain.
NMDA receptors bind glutamate.
trick: Sympathetic: short preganglionic fiber, norepinephrine at the target. Parasympathetic: acetylcholine at both synapses, muscarinic at the target.

q: Sympathetic postganglionic neurons release:
why: Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine onto their target organs.
traps: ACh is released by all preganglionic neurons and by parasympathetic postganglionic ones.
Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the brain.
Dopamine acts mainly in brain pathways.
trick: Sympathetic: short preganglionic fiber, norepinephrine at the target. Parasympathetic: acetylcholine at both synapses, muscarinic at the target.

q: Dopamine deficiency in substantia nigra causes:
why: Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra disrupts movement control and causes the tremor and slowness of Parkinson disease.
traps: Alzheimer disease involves loss of acetylcholine neurons and memory decline.
Huntington disease is a genetic loss of neurons in the striatum.
Multiple sclerosis is damage to myelin.
trick: Dopamine and substantia nigra: Parkinson.

q: GABA is the main:
why: GABA opens chloride channels, which makes neurons less likely to fire. It is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain.
traps: Glutamate is the main excitatory one.
Norepinephrine is the sympathetic transmitter.
Melatonin is the sleep hormone.
trick: Brain balance: glutamate excites, GABA inhibits.

q: Cerebellum primarily controls:
why: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, posture and balance by comparing intended movement with what is happening.
traps: Memory formation depends on the hippocampus.
Vision is processed in the occipital lobe.
Hormone release is run by the hypothalamus and pituitary.
trick: Cerebellum = coordination. Cerebrum = thought. Brainstem = vital functions.

q: Hypothalamus is critical for:
why: The hypothalamus monitors temperature, hunger, thirst and hormone levels and corrects them, partly by controlling the pituitary.
traps: The thalamus is the sensory relay.
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
The motor cortex initiates movement.
trick: Hypothalamus = homeostasis headquarters. Thalamus = relay station.

q: Multiple sclerosis attacks:
why: In multiple sclerosis the immune system attacks myelin in the brain and spinal cord, which slows or blocks nerve signals.
traps: The cell bodies are not the primary target.
Synapses are the target in myasthenia gravis, not MS.
Muscle weakness in MS comes from slowed nerve signals, not from muscle damage.
trick: MS = myelin of the central nervous system.

q: Glomerular filtration is driven by:
why: Blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries pushes water and small solutes through the filter into Bowman's capsule. No energy is spent by the filter itself.
traps: Active transport is used later, in reabsorption and secretion.
Diffusion alone would be far too slow.
Aquaporins act in reabsorption along the tubule.
trick: Filtration is pushed by pressure; reabsorption is pulled by transport.

q: PCT reabsorbs how much filtered Na+?
why: The proximal tubule reclaims about two thirds of the filtered sodium, along with nearly all the glucose and amino acids.
traps: Far too low; that is nearer the share handled by the collecting duct.
That is about the share reabsorbed by the loop of Henle.
That is the total across the whole nephron, not the proximal tubule alone.
trick: Proximal tubule = bulk reabsorption, about two thirds of salt and water.

q: Renin is released by kidney in response to:
why: Cells next to the glomerulus release renin when pressure or sodium delivery falls. Renin starts the chain that makes angiotensin II, which raises pressure.
traps: High pressure shuts renin off.
Glucose is handled by insulin and glucagon.
Low oxygen makes the kidney release erythropoietin, a different hormone.
trick: Renin = the kidney's response to low pressure.

q: Angiotensin II effects include:
why: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure two ways: it constricts arterioles directly, and it triggers aldosterone release so the kidney keeps sodium and water.
traps: It constricts vessels; it does not widen them.
Every action it has raises pressure.
Through aldosterone it causes sodium to be retained.
trick: Angiotensin II: squeeze the vessels and save the salt.

q: Glucose in urine (glucosuria) usually indicates:
why: Glucose is filtered freely and then reclaimed by carriers in the proximal tubule. The carriers can be saturated, so when blood glucose is very high (as in diabetes), the excess stays in the urine.
traps: Normally all filtered glucose is reclaimed.
Glucose is small and always filters; the filter is not the issue.
In kidney failure little is filtered at all.
trick: Carrier-based reabsorption has a ceiling (transport maximum).

q: Anterior pituitary makes which hormones?
opts: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin
why: The anterior pituitary makes six hormones: FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, prolactin and growth hormone.
traps: Those are made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
Those come from the pancreas.
Those come from the thyroid.
trick: Posterior pituitary only stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, which the hypothalamus makes. Everything else pituitary is anterior.

q: TSH stimulates:
why: Thyroid-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary tells the thyroid to make and release T3 and T4.
traps: The adrenal cortex is stimulated by ACTH.
TSH comes from the pituitary; it does not act on it.
The gonads are stimulated by FSH and LH.
trick: Tropic hormones are named for their target: TSH thyroid, ACTH adrenal cortex.

q: Cortisol is released from:
why: Cortisol is a steroid made by the adrenal cortex when ACTH arrives from the pituitary.
traps: The anterior pituitary makes ACTH, the signal for cortisol, not cortisol itself.
The adrenal medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine.
The pancreas makes insulin and glucagon.
trick: Adrenal cortex = steroids (cortisol, aldosterone). Adrenal medulla = epinephrine.

q: Steroid hormones bind:
why: Steroids are lipid-soluble, so they cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell. The hormone-receptor pair then acts on DNA to change which genes are transcribed.
traps: Surface receptors serve hormones that cannot cross the membrane, such as peptides.
Receptor tyrosine kinases bind peptides such as insulin.
Ion channel receptors bind neurotransmitters.
trick: Steroid hormones: cross the membrane, change gene expression, act slowly and for a long time.

q: Glucagon mobilizes glucose by:
why: Glucagon tells the liver to break glycogen into glucose and to build new glucose from other molecules, raising blood sugar between meals.
traps: Glycolysis uses glucose up.
Insulin lowers blood glucose, the opposite effect.
GLUT4 insertion is how insulin pulls glucose into cells.
trick: Glucagon: glucose gone, so release it. Insulin: glucose in, so store it.

q: Diabetes Type 1 results from:
why: In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells, so little or no insulin is made.
traps: Resistance to insulin describes type 2.
Glucagon excess is not the cause.
Lifestyle factors are tied to type 2.
trick: Type 1: no insulin made. Type 2: insulin made but cells respond poorly.

q: Melatonin is produced by:
why: The pineal gland releases melatonin in darkness, which helps set the sleep-wake cycle.
traps: The hypothalamus holds the body clock but does not make melatonin.
The thymus matures T cells.
The liver makes no melatonin.
trick: For any hormone, pin down three things: where it is made, what triggers it, what it does.

q: PTH effects on calcium:
why: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium by freeing it from bone, reclaiming it in the kidney and activating vitamin D so the gut absorbs more.
traps: Lowering calcium is the job of calcitonin.
Calcium control is its main job.
It makes the kidney keep calcium, not lose it.
trick: Calcium: PTH pulls it up, calcitonin tones it down.

q: Slow-twitch (Type I) muscle fibers are:
why: Slow-twitch fibers run on aerobic respiration. They are packed with mitochondria and myoglobin (which makes them red) and can work for long periods.
traps: That describes fast-twitch type IIb fibers.
Red color goes with oxidative metabolism, not glycolytic.
Oxidative fibers are red because of myoglobin.
trick: Slow = red, oxidative, endurance. Fast = white, glycolytic, power.

q: Cardiac muscle has intercalated discs that contain:
why: Intercalated discs join heart cells end to end. Desmosomes hold them together against the pull of each beat, and gap junctions let the electrical signal pass directly from cell to cell.
traps: Tight junctions seal sheets of cells; they are not what the discs are known for.
Heart cells are coupled electrically, not by chemical synapses.
Z lines mark sarcomere ends inside a cell.
trick: Gap junctions let the heart beat as one unit.

q: Rigor mortis occurs because:
why: A myosin head lets go of actin only when a new ATP binds. After death ATP runs out, so the heads stay locked on and the muscle goes rigid.
traps: Calcium in fact leaks out and exposes binding sites; the problem is that heads cannot release.
Acid build-up does not lock the cross-bridges.
Swelling is not the cause of stiffness.
trick: ATP is needed to let go, not just to pull.

q: Creatine phosphate provides:
why: Creatine phosphate hands its phosphate to ADP to remake ATP at once. The store lasts only about ten seconds of all-out effort.
traps: Long efforts rely on aerobic respiration.
Glycogen is the glucose store.
It does not buffer lactate.
trick: Energy order in muscle: stored ATP, creatine phosphate, glycolysis, aerobic respiration.

q: Lactose is digested by:
why: Lactase, an enzyme on the brush border of the small intestine, splits lactose into glucose and galactose.
traps: Amylase works on starch.
Pepsin works on protein.
Bile emulsifies fat and digests nothing.
trick: Enzyme names follow their substrate: lactase lactose, sucrase sucrose, maltase maltose.

q: Salivary amylase begins digestion of:
why: Amylase in saliva starts breaking starch into smaller sugars while food is still in the mouth.
traps: Protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin.
Fat digestion happens mainly in the small intestine.
Nucleic acids are broken down by pancreatic nucleases.
trick: Match enzyme, source and target: amylase starch, pepsin protein in acid, lipase fat with bile, brush border enzymes finish the job.

q: Pepsin requires what to be active?
why: Pepsin is made as inactive pepsinogen and is switched on by stomach acid. It works best near pH 2.
traps: Basic conditions in the small intestine shut pepsin off.
Bile acts in the small intestine on fats.
Calcium is not what activates it.
trick: Match enzyme, source and target: amylase starch, pepsin protein in acid, lipase fat with bile, brush border enzymes finish the job.

q: Most nutrients are absorbed in the:
why: Villi and microvilli give the small intestine an enormous surface, and almost all nutrient absorption happens there.
traps: The stomach mostly mixes and begins protein digestion.
The large intestine absorbs water and salts.
The esophagus only moves food along.
trick: Small intestine absorbs nutrients; large intestine absorbs water.

q: CCK (cholecystokinin) triggers:
why: Fat and protein entering the small intestine trigger CCK, which makes the gallbladder contract and the pancreas release its enzymes.
traps: Acid release is driven by gastrin.
CCK slows stomach emptying.
Insulin responds to blood glucose.
trick: Gut hormones: gastrin acid, secretin bicarbonate, CCK bile and enzymes.

q: Vitamin K is produced in humans by:
why: Bacteria in the large intestine make vitamin K, which adds to what comes from leafy greens in the diet.
traps: The liver uses vitamin K to make clotting factors but does not make the vitamin.
The kidney is not a source.
Diet is one source, but intestinal bacteria supply some too.
trick: Vitamin K: from greens and gut bacteria, used by the liver for clotting.

q: NK (natural killer) cells are part of:
why: Natural killer cells attack virus-infected and abnormal cells right away, with no prior exposure and no antigen-specific receptor. That makes them innate.
traps: Adaptive cells need days and recognize one specific antigen.
B cells make antibodies.
T cells carry antigen-specific receptors; NK cells do not.
trick: Innate = fast and general. Adaptive = slow, specific, with memory.

q: IgM is significant because:
why: IgM is the first antibody class secreted in a new infection. It is a pentamer, five units joined together, so it grabs antigens well even before the response matures.
traps: That is IgG.
That is IgE.
IgM is the largest antibody.
trick: Antibody classes: G crosses the placenta, A guards mucosa, M comes first, E allergies, D sits on B cells.

q: IgE is associated with:
why: IgE sits on mast cells and triggers histamine release. That reaction drives allergies and helps fight parasitic worms.
traps: IgG and IgM handle most bacterial defense.
IgA protects mucosal surfaces.
IgD and IgM serve as B cell receptors.
trick: Antibody classes: G crosses the placenta, A guards mucosa, M comes first, E allergies, D sits on B cells.

q: Vaccines work by:
why: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form of an antigen. The body makes memory B and T cells, so a later real infection meets a fast, strong response.
traps: That is passive immunity, which leaves no memory.
A vaccine contains nothing that kills microbes.
Antibiotics are drugs that attack bacteria.
trick: Vaccine = practice run that leaves memory cells (active immunity).

q: Active vs passive immunity: passive immunity:
why: Passive immunity means receiving antibodies made by someone else, such as across the placenta or in an antiserum. Protection is immediate but fades as the antibodies break down.
traps: It is short-lived because no memory cells form.
Vaccination produces active immunity.
No memory cells are involved.
trick: Active: you make the antibodies (slow, lasting). Passive: you are given them (fast, brief).

q: Menstrual cycle phase with peak progesterone:
why: After ovulation the emptied follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which pours out progesterone. That stage is the luteal phase.
traps: Estrogen dominates the follicular phase.
Hormone levels are at their lowest during menstruation.
Ovulation is marked by the LH surge.
trick: Menstrual cycle: FSH grows the follicle, estrogen rises, the LH surge releases the egg, the corpus luteum makes progesterone.

q: Spermatogenesis takes place in:
why: Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules of the testes.
traps: The vas deferens carries sperm toward the urethra.
The epididymis is where sperm mature and are stored.
Both glands add fluid to semen; neither makes sperm.
trick: Sperm path: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra.

q: Primary oocytes are arrested in:
why: Every primary oocyte starts meiosis before birth and stops in prophase I. It resumes years later, just before it is ovulated.
traps: No arrest happens in anaphase II.
Metaphase II is the second pause, in the secondary oocyte, until fertilization.
Meiosis has already begun, so the cell is past G1.
trick: Sperm: continuous from puberty, four per meiosis. Eggs: started before birth, paused twice, one per meiosis.

q: How many viable gametes per meiosis in females?
why: Both meiotic divisions split the cytoplasm unevenly. One large egg keeps nearly all of it, and the small polar bodies break down.
traps: Four is the count for sperm.
The second division also yields one polar body, not a second egg.
Meiosis makes four cells at most.
trick: Sperm: continuous from puberty, four per meiosis. Eggs: started before birth, paused twice, one per meiosis.

q: FSH in males stimulates:
why: FSH acts on Sertoli cells, which nourish developing sperm and support spermatogenesis.
traps: Testosterone production is driven by LH acting on Leydig cells.
Erection is a parasympathetic reflex.
Ejaculation is a sympathetic reflex.
trick: Male pairs: LH with Leydig cells (testosterone), FSH with Sertoli cells (sperm support).

q: Stratum that contains stem cells:
why: The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis. Its stem cells divide constantly to replace the cells shed at the surface.
traps: The corneum is the dead outer layer.
The granulosum is where cells fill with keratin and die.
The lucidum is a thin clear layer found only in thick skin.
trick: Epidermis from deep to surface: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum.

q: Sweat glands are most concentrated in:
why: Eccrine sweat glands are packed most densely on the palms and the soles of the feet.
traps: The back has many glands in total but at a lower density.
The lips have no sweat glands.
The eyelids have few.
trick: Densest sweat glands: palms and soles.

q: Long bone shaft is the:
why: The diaphysis is the long central shaft of a long bone.
traps: The epiphysis is the rounded end.
The metaphysis is the zone between shaft and end, where the growth plate sits.
The periosteum is the membrane covering the bone.
trick: Long bone parts: epiphysis (ends), metaphysis (growth plate), diaphysis (shaft).

q: Compact bone's structural unit:
why: Compact bone is built from osteons: cylinders of concentric rings around a central canal that carries vessels and nerves.
traps: Trabeculae are the struts of spongy bone.
Lamellae are the rings within an osteon, not the whole unit.
Lacunae are the small spaces that hold osteocytes.
trick: Compact bone = osteons. Spongy bone = trabeculae.

q: Endochondral ossification builds:
why: In endochondral ossification a cartilage model forms first and is gradually replaced by bone. Most of the skeleton, including the long bones, forms this way.
traps: Flat skull bones form directly in membrane (intramembranous ossification).
Enamel is not bone.
Joint surfaces keep their cartilage.
trick: Endochondral = cartilage first (long bones). Intramembranous = direct (flat skull bones).

q: Hinge joints are best example:
why: A hinge joint swings in one plane, like a door: bend and straighten. The elbow and the knee work this way.
traps: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint.
The thumb base is a saddle joint.
Vertebrae are joined by cartilage discs and gliding joints.
trick: Hinge = one plane (elbow, knee). Ball and socket = all planes (hip, shoulder).

q: Ductus arteriosus connects:
why: Blood that does reach the fetal pulmonary artery is diverted through this vessel into the aorta, so it skips the lungs.
traps: That is the foramen ovale.
Direction reversed. Before birth, pressure is higher on the pulmonary side.
That is the ductus venosus, which bypasses the liver.
trick: Two fetal shortcuts skip the lungs: foramen ovale (right atrium to left atrium) and ductus arteriosus (pulmonary artery to aorta).

q: Countercurrent multiplier in kidney refers to:
opts: The loop building a salt gradient
why: Fluid runs in opposite directions in the two limbs of the loop of Henle. The ascending limb pumps out salt, the descending limb loses water, and together they build a steep salt gradient in the medulla.
traps: Filtration happens before the loop.
Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct.
Blood flow supplies the kidney but is not the multiplier.
trick: The loop makes the medulla salty; the collecting duct uses that gradient to concentrate urine.

q: Growth hormone deficiency in children causes:
why: Too little growth hormone during childhood slows bone growth and leads to short stature with normal body proportions.
traps: Acromegaly is too much growth hormone in adults.
Cretinism is from too little thyroid hormone in infancy.
Diabetes mellitus involves insulin.
trick: GH: too little in childhood dwarfism, too much in childhood gigantism, too much in adults acromegaly.

q: Cytotoxic T cells (CD8) recognize:
why: CD8 cytotoxic T cells check MHC I, found on every nucleated cell, which displays fragments of proteins made inside that cell. A viral fragment there marks the cell for killing.
traps: MHC II is read by CD4 helper T cells.
T cells do not recognize surface antibodies.
T cells only see antigen presented on MHC; B cells bind free antigen.
trick: MHC I is on all nucleated cells and talks to CD8 cells (1 x 8 = 8). MHC II is on antigen-presenting cells and talks to CD4 cells (2 x 4 = 8).

q: Brainstem includes:
why: The brainstem is made of the midbrain, pons and medulla. It links the brain to the spinal cord and runs breathing, heart rate and other basics.
traps: The cerebellum sits behind the brainstem and is separate from it.
The cerebrum is the large upper brain.
The hypothalamus is part of the diencephalon, above the brainstem.
trick: Cerebellum = coordination. Cerebrum = thought. Brainstem = vital functions.

q: Androgens are produced in females by:
why: Women make small amounts of androgens in the ovaries and in the adrenal cortex. Much of it is converted to estrogen.
traps: Females do make androgens, in small amounts.
The pituitary makes the signals (LH, ACTH), not the steroids.
The placenta exists only in pregnancy.
trick: Both sexes make both sex steroids; the amounts differ.

q: Which feature is shared by Archaea + Eukarya but NOT Bacteria?
why: Archaea and eukaryotes both wrap DNA around histone proteins. Bacteria lack histones.
traps: Peptidoglycan is found only in bacteria.
70S ribosomes are found in bacteria and archaea, not in the eukaryotic cytoplasm.
A single circular chromosome is typical of bacteria and archaea.
trick: Archaea look like bacteria but handle DNA more like eukaryotes.

q: Which is NOT characteristic of Fungi?
why: Fungal walls are made of chitin. Cellulose walls belong to plants.
traps: Chitin walls are a defining fungal trait.
Fungi digest food outside their bodies and absorb it.
Fungi store glycogen, as animals do.
trick: Fungi: chitin walls, absorb food, store glycogen. Plants: cellulose walls, starch.

q: Bryophytes (mosses) are unique among plants in being:
why: In mosses the green plant you see is the haploid gametophyte, and the sporophyte is a small stalk that depends on it. Every other plant group has the sporophyte as the main stage.
traps: Mosses have no true vascular tissue.
Sporophyte dominance describes ferns and seed plants.
Mosses reproduce with spores, not seeds.
trick: Plant ladder: mosses (no vessels, gametophyte dominant), ferns (vessels, no seeds), gymnosperms (naked seeds), angiosperms (flowers, fruit).

q: In angiosperm double fertilization, endosperm is:
why: One sperm fertilizes the egg to make the diploid zygote. A second sperm joins two polar nuclei in the central cell, giving 1 + 2 = 3 sets: triploid endosperm.
traps: Gametes are haploid.
The zygote is diploid; the endosperm has one more set.
Only three nuclei fuse, not four.
trick: Double fertilization: sperm + egg = 2n embryo; sperm + two polar nuclei = 3n endosperm.

q: Pseudocoelomates have body cavity:
opts: Lined by mesoderm on all sides
why: A pseudocoelom is a fluid-filled cavity with mesoderm on its outer side only; the inner side is the endoderm of the gut.
traps: A cavity fully lined by mesoderm is a true coelom.
No cavity describes acoelomates such as flatworms.
The cavity sits inside the mesoderm, next to the gut.
trick: Body cavity: acoelomate has none, pseudocoelomate has one only partly lined by mesoderm, coelomate has one fully lined.

q: Which phylum is characterized by the water vascular system?
why: Sea stars and their relatives move, feed and breathe using a network of water-filled canals that power their tube feet.
traps: Annelids are segmented worms that move with muscles and bristles.
Molluscs use a muscular foot.
Arthropods use jointed legs.
trick: Water vascular system and tube feet: echinoderms.

q: An organism with spiral, determinate cleavage is a:
why: Spiral cleavage in which each cell's fate is fixed early (determinate) is the protostome pattern.
traps: Deuterostomes have radial, indeterminate cleavage.
The pattern clearly matches one group.
The two groups differ on exactly this point.
trick: Protostome: mouth first, spiral and determinate cleavage. Deuterostome: anus first, radial and indeterminate cleavage.

q: Which group includes echinoderms + chordates?
why: Echinoderms and chordates share the deuterostome pattern: the blastopore becomes the anus, and cleavage is radial and indeterminate.
traps: Protostomes include molluscs, annelids and arthropods.
Lophotrochozoa is a protostome group (molluscs, annelids).
Ecdysozoa is a protostome group (arthropods, nematodes).
trick: Protostome: mouth first, spiral and determinate cleavage. Deuterostome: anus first, radial and indeterminate cleavage.

q: Monocots vs dicots: which is monocot trait?
why: Monocots have one seed leaf, parallel veins, flower parts in threes, scattered vascular bundles and fibrous roots.
traps: Two cotyledons is the dicot trait the group is named for.
Netted veins are a dicot trait.
A taproot is a dicot trait; monocots have fibrous roots.
trick: Monocot: one cotyledon, parallel veins, parts in threes. Dicot: two, netted, fours or fives.

q: Bird wings + insect wings are an example of:
why: Both wings are for flying, but birds and insects evolved them separately from different starting parts. Same job, different origin is analogous.
traps: Homologous structures share an origin, like a bird wing and a human arm.
Vestigial structures have lost their function; both wings work.
A shared derived trait is inherited from a common ancestor that had it.
trick: Vestigial = leftover from an ancestor. Homologous = same origin. Analogous = same job.

q: A clade containing ancestor + ALL descendants is:
why: A monophyletic group, or clade, is one ancestor and every one of its descendants, with nothing left out and nothing extra.
traps: A polyphyletic group lumps species from different ancestors.
A paraphyletic group has the ancestor but leaves out some descendants.
That is not a term used for groups on a tree.
trick: Mono = the whole branch. Para = branch with a piece cut off. Poly = pieces of different branches.

q: Lichens are:
opts: A fungus living with an alga
why: A lichen is a partnership: a fungus gives structure and holds water, and a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium inside it makes food.
traps: A lichen is two organisms from different kingdoms.
Lichens make their own food through their partner and do not feed on the tree.
Slime molds are protists.
trick: Lichen = fungus + photosynthetic partner (mutualism).

q: Sponges (Porifera) are unique because they:
why: Sponges are animals whose cells are not organized into true tissues or organs.
traps: Most sponges have no symmetry, and radial symmetry is the cnidarian trait.
Sponges branch off before the protostome and deuterostome split.
Sponges have no body cavity.
trick: Sponges: no tissues, no symmetry, filter feeders.

q: Cnidarians are:
why: Cnidarians such as jellyfish form only two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with jelly-like material between them.
traps: Three germ layers appear in bilateral animals.
Cnidarians are radial, not bilateral.
Deuterostomes are bilateral animals with three layers.
trick: Two layers and radial: cnidarians. Three layers and bilateral: everything from flatworms up.

q: Gymnosperms' main innovation over seedless vascular plants:
why: Gymnosperms package the embryo in a seed and deliver sperm by airborne pollen, so they no longer need water for fertilization.
traps: Ferns already have vascular tissue.
Flowers are the angiosperm innovation.
Fruit is the angiosperm innovation; gymnosperm seeds are exposed.
trick: Plant ladder: mosses (no vessels, gametophyte dominant), ferns (vessels, no seeds), gymnosperms (naked seeds), angiosperms (flowers, fruit).

q: An organism with bilateral larva but radial adult is most likely a/an:
why: Echinoderm larvae are bilateral, which shows their bilateral ancestry. The adult body is rebuilt with five-part radial symmetry.
traps: Cnidarians are radial at every stage.
Sponges have no true symmetry.
Molluscs are bilateral as adults.
trick: Echinoderms: bilateral larva, radial adult.

q: Earthworm vs grasshopper circulation:
why: Annelids such as earthworms keep blood inside vessels (closed). Arthropods such as grasshoppers pump fluid into open body spaces that bathe the organs (open).
traps: Earthworm blood stays in vessels.
Grasshopper fluid leaves the vessels.
Reversed: the earthworm is the one with the closed system.
trick: Closed circulation: annelids, cephalopods, vertebrates. Open: arthropods and most molluscs.

q: Triploblastic animals possess:
why: Triploblastic animals form ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. The added middle layer makes muscle and organs possible.
traps: Two layers is diploblastic, as in cnidarians.
No animal has four germ layers.
No tissues describes sponges.
trick: Germ layers: ectoderm = skin and nervous system, mesoderm = muscle, bone, blood and kidneys, endoderm = gut lining and its glands.

q: Acoelomate phylum example:
why: Flatworms have solid bodies with no cavity between the gut and the body wall.
traps: Annelids have a true coelom.
Nematodes have a pseudocoelom.
Molluscs have a (reduced) true coelom.
trick: Body cavity: acoelomate has none, pseudocoelomate has one only partly lined by mesoderm, coelomate has one fully lined.

q: Pseudocoelomate phylum:
why: Roundworms have a body cavity that is lined by mesoderm only on the outside, which makes it a pseudocoelom.
traps: Flatworms have no body cavity.
Annelids have a true coelom.
Molluscs have a true coelom.
trick: Body cavity: acoelomate has none, pseudocoelomate has one only partly lined by mesoderm, coelomate has one fully lined.

q: Sponges feed using:
why: Choanocytes line the inside of a sponge. Their beating flagella pull water through, and their collars trap food particles.
traps: Tentacles belong to cnidarians.
A pharynx is a flatworm feature.
Sponges have no mouth.
trick: Sponges: no tissues, no symmetry, filter feeders.

q: Cnidocytes are characteristic of:
why: Cnidocytes are the stinging cells of jellyfish, corals and anemones. Each fires a tiny harpoon to catch prey, and they give the phylum its name.
traps: Sponges filter feed with collar cells.
Flatworms have no stinging cells.
Roundworms have no stinging cells.
trick: Cnidocyte, Cnidaria: the name tells you.

q: Class Insecta defining traits:
why: Insects have three body regions (head, thorax, abdomen) and three pairs of legs on the thorax. Most also have wings.
traps: That describes arachnids.
That describes decapod crustaceans such as crabs.
That describes centipedes and millipedes.
trick: Arthropod count: insects 6 legs and 3 body parts, arachnids 8 legs and 2 body parts, crustaceans branched limbs.

q: Spiders are class:
why: Spiders have eight legs and two body regions, which places them in Arachnida with scorpions, ticks and mites.
traps: Insects have six legs and three body regions.
Crustaceans are mostly aquatic with branched limbs.
Diplopoda are the millipedes.
trick: Arthropod count: insects 6 legs and 3 body parts, arachnids 8 legs and 2 body parts, crustaceans branched limbs.

q: Crustaceans differ from insects in:
why: Crustacean limbs are biramous, meaning each splits into two branches, and they have two pairs of antennae. Insect limbs are unbranched.
traps: All arthropods have an exoskeleton.
Size does not separate the groups.
All arthropods molt.
trick: Arthropod count: insects 6 legs and 3 body parts, arachnids 8 legs and 2 body parts, crustaceans branched limbs.

q: Centipedes vs millipedes:
opts: One leg pair per segment against two
why: Centipedes have one pair of legs on each segment and are fast predators with venom claws. Millipedes have two pairs per segment and eat decaying plants.
traps: They are separate classes.
Segment count does not separate them; legs per segment does.
Centipedes are the venomous ones.
trick: Centipede: 1 pair per segment, predator. Millipede: 2 pairs, plant eater.

q: Chordate features (at some life stage):
why: All chordates have, at some stage, a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and a tail that extends past the anus.
traps: Only vertebrates have a backbone; some chordates never do.
Many other phyla are bilateral.
Many other phyla have a coelom.
trick: Four chordate marks: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail.

q: Amphibian skin:
why: Amphibians have thin, moist skin that gases pass through, so they do part of their breathing through it. It also ties them to damp places.
traps: Dry scaly skin is reptilian.
Feathers belong to birds.
Fur belongs to mammals.
trick: Amphibians: moist skin breathing, eggs in water.

q: Reptilian innovation that allowed full terrestrial life:
why: The amniotic egg carries its own water supply and membranes inside a shell, so reptiles could reproduce on dry land. Waterproof scaly skin completed the move.
traps: Amphibians and some fish already had lungs.
Reptiles are ectotherms.
Hair is a mammal trait.
trick: Amniotic egg = reproduction freed from water.

q: Mammal defining traits:
why: Every mammal has hair and feeds its young with milk from mammary glands. No other group has either.
traps: Reptiles, birds and amphibians have lungs too.
Birds are also endotherms.
Some mammals lay eggs, and some fish and reptiles bear live young.
trick: Mammal = hair + milk. Everything else has exceptions.

q: Birds are taxonomically:

Mammals split off from a different early amniote line.
Birds are amniotes, well removed from amphibians.

Sharks are fish with gills, not reptiles.

Sharks and rays have jaws.
Lampreys are fish.

Most protozoa are motile.

Maternal age effect for Down syndrome:

why: A woman's oocytes have been paused in meiosis since before her birth. The longer they wait, the more likely chromosomes fail to separate properly, so the chance of trisomy 21 climbs with her age.

The trend runs the other way.
